              <div class="be__contents-wrapper">
                <h2><a id="post-168583-_4lt92rr5muov"></a>Executive Summary</h2>
<p>RansomHouse is a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation run by a group that we track as Jolly Scorpius. Recent samples of the associated binaries used in RansomHouse operations reveal a significant upgrade in encryption. This article explores the upgrade of RansomHouse encryption and the potential impact for defenders.</p>
<p>Jolly Scorpius uses a double extortion strategy. This strategy combines stealing and encrypting a victim's data with threats to leak the stolen data.</p>
<p>The scale of the group's operations is significant. At the time of this article, at least 123 victims were listed on the RansomHouse data leak site as having their data disclosed or sold since December 2021.</p>
<p>This group has disrupted critical sectors including healthcare, finance, transportation and government. The consequences of these intrusions include significant financial losses, major data breaches and erosion of public trust in the affected organizations.</p>
<p>To better understand RansomHouse operations, we review its attack chain. We also examine the upgrade to this ransomware's encryption from a simple, single-phase linear technique to a more complex, multi-layered method.</p>
<p>Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats described in this article through the following products and services:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/wildfire" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced WildFire</a></li>
<li><a href="https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/cortex/cortex-xpanse" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cortex Xpanse</a> and the <a href="https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/cortex/cortex-xsiam" target="_blank" rel="noopener">ASM add-on for XSIAM</a></li>
</ul>
<p>If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the <a href="https://start.paloaltonetworks.com/contact-unit42.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Unit 42 Incident Response team</a>.</p>
<table style="width: 100%;">
<thead>
<tr>
<td style="width: 35%;"><b>Related Unit 42 Topics</b></td>
<td style="width: 100%;"><a href="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/category/ransomware/" target="_blank" rel="noopener"><b>Ransomware</b></a>, <strong><a href="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tag/esxi/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">ESXi</a></strong></td>
</tr>
</thead>
</table>
<h2><a id="post-168583-_wven14kmgum2"></a>Actor Roles and the Attack Chain</h2>
<p>Despite Jolly Scorpius positioning itself as a group that exposes corporate vulnerabilities, its actions reveal a straightforward extortion business. To better understand its RansomHouse operations, we can identify the specific actor roles, discern separate phases of the attack chain and determine how the roles and phases relate to each other.</p>
<p>Figure 1 illustrates these roles and their positions in the attack chain.</p>
<figure id="attachment_168596" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-168596" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-168596 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-624243-168583-1.png" alt="Diagram of the RansomHouse attack chain with two sections titled &quot;Roles and Attack Chain&quot;. Under &quot;Roles,&quot; there are icons representing an Operator, an Attacker, and a Victim. Below, the &quot;Attack Chain&quot; is divided into four steps: 1. Develop, showing icons for Tools and Leak website. 2. Infiltrate, indicating Initial access and Lateral movement. 3. Exfiltrate &amp; Deploy, with icons for MrAgent and Mario alongside VMWare. 4. Extort is symbolized by a server and communication between two persons. " width="1000" height="465" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-624243-168583-1.png 2048w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-624243-168583-1-786x366.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-624243-168583-1-1504x700.png 1504w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-624243-168583-1-768x357.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-624243-168583-1-1536x715.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-168596" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 1. Actor roles and how they relate to phases of the RansomHouse attack chain.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The RansomHouse attack chain involves three distinct roles:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Operator: </strong>Operates the RaaS</li>
<li><strong>Attacker: </strong>Deploys the ransomware</li>
<li><strong>Victim: </strong>Targeted by the attacker</li>
</ul>
<p>Operators are responsible for establishing and maintaining the RaaS, including the development of tools for data encryption and other functions. Individuals in this role manage the data leak site and architecture for victims to negotiate ransom payments. This includes managing the cryptocurrency wallets for ransom collection and laundering.</p>
<p>Attackers are typically known as affiliates because they are separate threat actors from the operators. As ransomware services rise and fall, attackers can switch their affiliation to different RaaS groups. Attackers are responsible for gaining initial access, moving laterally, exfiltrating data and deploying the ransomware.</p>
<p>Attackers for RansomHouse are <a href="https://www.scworld.com/news/mragent-ransomware-tool-from-ransomhouse-group-targets-esxi-servers" target="_blank" rel="noopener">known for targeting VMware ESXi infrastructure</a>, a common enterprise-grade hypervisor platform. RansomHouse attackers specifically target ESXi because compromising this platform allows them to encrypt dozens or hundreds of virtual machines at once, causing maximum operational disruption.</p>
<p>The attack chain reflects a multi-faceted strategy to pressure RansomHouse victims. This strategy involves harvesting sensitive information, encrypting select data, publishing victim identities and threatening to release their sensitive data. The RansomHouse attack chain can be broken into four phases:</p>
<ol>
<li>Develop</li>
<li>Infiltrate</li>
<li>Exfiltrate and deploy</li>
<li>Extort</li>
</ol>
<p>Each phase involves at least one of the three roles.</p>
<h3><a id="post-168583-_hcc7cm6zd1ql"></a>Phase 1: Develop</h3>
<p>In this phase, RansomHouse operators function as the backend providers, responsible for developing all aspects of the RaaS. Crucially, the operators typically do not conduct the initial intrusions. Instead, they rely on their affiliates (i.e., the attackers) to leverage the RaaS services developed in this phase.</p>
<h3><a id="post-168583-_rkbgbjfxn5sw"></a>Phase 2: Infiltrate</h3>
<p>In this phase, attackers compromise victims through spear phishing emails or other social engineering techniques. In addition to email, initial access vectors include vulnerable systems in a victim's environment that attackers can compromise through zero-day or other exploits.</p>
<p>After achieving initial access, attackers typically use third-party tools and frameworks to explore the victim's network. The remainder of the infiltration phase includes reconnaissance to map the environment, privilege escalation, lateral movement and identifying valuable or sensitive information.</p>
<h3><a id="post-168583-_tm1944cwtaa5"></a>Phase 3: Exfiltrate and Deplo<strong>y</strong></h3>
<p>Once attackers affiliated with RansomHouse have infiltrated a victim's environment, they exfiltrate sensitive data and deploy the ransomware. Typical data exfiltration techniques involve file compression and file transfer utilities, and attackers usually send data to servers under their control.</p>
<p>The RansomHouse RaaS uses a modular architecture that consists of two components:</p>
<ul>
<li>Management tool</li>
<li>Encryptor</li>
</ul>
<p>RansomHouse uses a management tool called MrAgent, designed to <a href="https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/ransomhouse-am-see/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">automate and track ransomware deployments across different hypervisor systems</a> in an ESXi environment.</p>
<p>RansomHouse uses an encryptor known as Mario. After encrypting files, Mario drops a ransom note that contains instructions on how victims can recover their data.</p>
<h3><a id="post-168583-_8ihcjwvqnf5e"></a>Phase 4: Extort</h3>
<p>Once a victim's data has been stolen and encrypted, the attack chain transitions to the extortion phase. RaaS operators are generally responsible for this phase, which often involves negotiations via dedicated chat rooms. Operators validate their threats through strategic information disclosure on platforms like Telegram and the RansomHouse data leak site.</p>
<p>Now that we better understand the RansomHouse attack chain, let's review how the components of this ransomware are used in attacks.</p>
<h2><a id="post-168583-_25xn81m61ct0"></a>RansomHouse Components Used in Attacks</h2>
<p>The two components of this ransomware (i.e., MrAgent and Mario) are specifically engineered to compromise virtualized environments. Figure 2 illustrates how these tools are used in a RansomHouse attack in an ESXi network.</p>
<figure id="attachment_168607" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-168607" style="width: 900px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-168607 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-627791-168583-2.png" alt="Flowchart showing a cybersecurity attack process. Includes an &quot;Attacker (RansomHouse) C2 Server&quot; connecting and sending commands, which deploy deployment tools and ransomware via &quot;VMware ESXi Hypervisor&quot; to target &quot;Virtualized Datastores&quot; including &quot;VM Files&quot; like .vmdk and .vmx, affecting VMs designated as Web Server, Database, and Domain Controller." width="900" height="989" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-627791-168583-2.png 1863w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-627791-168583-2-400x440.png 400w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-627791-168583-2-637x700.png 637w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-627791-168583-2-768x844.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-627791-168583-2-1397x1536.png 1397w" sizes="(max-width: 900px) 100vw, 900px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-168607" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 2. Flow chart of how RansomHouse components are used in an ESXi environment.</figcaption></figure>
<p>After infiltrating the environment, an attacker deploys MrAgent onto the victim's ESXi hypervisor. MrAgent establishes a persistent connection to the attacker's command-and-control (C2) server.</p>
<p>Attackers then issue commands from the C2 server to MrAgent for further operations like data exfiltration. After the data is exfiltrated, attackers instruct MrAgent to download and execute the Mario encryptor, which runs directly on the hypervisor to encrypt virtual machine (VM) files.</p>
<p>Since MrAgent is the first component in the attack, let's review how it works.</p>
<h2><a id="post-168583-_3f3xtwwu3vj8"></a>MrAgent: The RansomHouse Deployment Tool</h2>
<p>As the primary tool for RansomHouse operations, MrAgent provides attackers with persistent access to a victim's environment and simplifies managing compromised hosts at scale. This management is accomplished through various functions of the tool.</p>
<h3><a id="post-168583-_wusv4h42aeu2"></a>Functions</h3>
<p>The main functions of MrAgent are:</p>
<ul>
<li>Acquiring host identifiers</li>
<li>Acquiring the host's IP address</li>
<li>Disabling the firewall</li>
<li>Communicating with the attacker's C2 server</li>
</ul>
<p>While <a href="https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/ransomhouse-am-see/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">an analysis by Trellix</a> has documented the commands MrAgent uses for these functions, we can review them to better understand its operations.</p>
<p>Commands for acquiring host identifiers are as follows:</p>
<ul>
<li>For the hostname: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">uname -a</span></li>
<li>For the MAC address: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">esxcli --formatter=csv network nic list</span></li>
</ul>
<p>The command to acquire the host's IP address is:</p>
<ul>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">esxcli --formatter=csv network ip interface ipv4 get</span></li>
</ul>
<p>The command to disable the firewall is:</p>
<ul>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">esxcli network firewall set --enabled false</span></li>
</ul>
<p>MrAgent's function to check for connectivity to the C2 server runs in an infinite loop. During these connectivity checks, MrAgent can receive various instructions from the C2 server. Table 1 lists examples of these instructions and their function.</p>
<table style="width: 100%;">
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; width: 21.875%;"><b>Instruction</b></td>
<td style="text-align: center; width: 77.4493%;"><b>Function</b></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="width: 21.875%;"><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Abort</span></td>
<td style="width: 77.4493%;"><span style="font-weight: 400;">Aborts the start of encryption if the hypervisor is in its delay phase after a reboot</span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="width: 21.875%;"><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Abort_f</span></td>
<td style="width: 77.4493%;"><span style="font-weight: 400;">Kills threads spawned by MrAgent</span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="width: 21.875%;"><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Config</span></td>
<td style="width: 77.4493%;"><span style="font-weight: 400;">Overwrites the local configuration used for ransomware deployment</span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="width: 21.875%;"><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Exec</span></td>
<td style="width: 77.4493%;"><span style="font-weight: 400;">Starts the ransomware deployment, changing the root password, disabling vCenter remote management via </span><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">/etc/init.d/vpxa stop</span><span style="font-weight: 400;"> and starting the encryption of VMs</span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="width: 21.875%;"><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Info</span></td>
<td style="width: 77.4493%;"><span style="font-weight: 400;">Retrieves ESXi host information</span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="width: 21.875%;"><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Run</span></td>
<td style="width: 77.4493%;"><span style="font-weight: 400;">Executes arbitrary commands on the ESXi host by writing to the file </span><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">./shmv</span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="width: 21.875%;"><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Remove</span></td>
<td style="width: 77.4493%;"><span style="font-weight: 400;">Removes content from the ESXi host by executing the command </span><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;"><span style="font-weight: 400;">rm -rf</span> <i><span style="font-weight: 400;">[filename or path]</span></i></span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="width: 21.875%;"><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Quit</span></td>
<td style="width: 77.4493%;"><span style="font-weight: 400;">Kills and removes the MrAgent binary using </span><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">rm -f</span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="width: 21.875%;"><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Welcome</span></td>
<td style="width: 77.4493%;"><span style="font-weight: 400;">Sets the ESXi welcome message on the host via </span><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;"><span style="font-weight: 400;">esxcli system welcomemesg set -m="</span><i><span style="font-weight: 400;">[text of message]</span></i><span style="font-weight: 400;">"</span></span></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><span style="font-size: 10pt;">Table 1. Examples of MrAgent instructions from an attacker's C2 server.</span></p>
<p>These functions enable MrAgent to deploy the Mario encryptor.</p>
<h3><a id="post-168583-_uzh2b8cepkg8"></a>Characteristics</h3>
<p>To impede reverse engineering, the MrAgent binary is sometimes modified with junk code, but this basic obfuscation does not alter its fundamental operations. For <a href="https://campus.barracuda.com/product/managedworkplace/doc/497818099/performing-guest-state-management-in-vmware" target="_blank" rel="noopener">state management</a> of the compromised environment, MrAgent uses two internal JSON structures to store its runtime configuration and status, with access synchronized by a mutex.</p>
<h2><a id="post-168583-_xml9k6jn1dub"></a>Mario: The RansomHouse Encryptor</h2>
<p>MrAgent deploys Mario to accomplish the operation's core function of encrypting critical VM files in the ESXi hypervisor. Our research uncovered two distinct versions of Mario that reveal an evolution in its encryption methods.</p>
<p>Both versions follow the same overall execution flow:</p>
<ol>
<li>Create the ransom note</li>
<li>Target file extensions</li>
<li>Encrypt files</li>
<li>Report statistics</li>
</ol>
<h3><a id="post-168583-_y3bob8xx780"></a>Creating the Ransom Note</h3>
<p>The first step in Mario's execution flow is creating a ransom note. The ransom note is named <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">How To Restore Your Files.txt</span> and is located in the directory of any files that Mario encrypts.</p>
<p>Mario opens the ransom note in write mode and saves text to the file that provides instructions for victims to recover their files. Figure 3 below shows an example of this note.</p>
<figure id="attachment_168618" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-168618" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-168618 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-631645-168583-3.png" alt="RansomHouse ransom note. Image of a text file titled &quot;How To Restore Your Files.txt&quot; open in Notepad with ASCII art depicting Super Mario alongside instructions for contacting a provided email and Telegram channel, indicating a ransomware notice from the group named &quot;RansomHouse.&quot;" width="1000" height="731" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-631645-168583-3.png 2048w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-631645-168583-3-602x440.png 602w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-631645-168583-3-957x700.png 957w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-631645-168583-3-768x562.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-631645-168583-3-1536x1124.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-168618" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 3. Example of a ransom note generated by <a href="https://www.virustotal.com/gui/file/0fe7fcc66726f8f2daed29b807d1da3c531ec004925625855f8889950d0d24d8" target="_blank" rel="noopener">a Mario sample</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<h3><a id="post-168583-_ylc1gm66x13b"></a>Targeting File Extensions</h3>
<p>The next step is directory traversal and extension targeting. Mario requires attackers to specify the directory path of the files to encrypt. Within the specified directory, Mario targets virtualization files based on the filename extensions listed in Table 2.</p>
<table>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center;"><b>Extension</b></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><b>File Description</b></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">ova</span></td>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400;">Open Virtual Appliance (OVA): a single-file distribution of the OVF file package</span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">ovf</span></td>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400;">Open Virtualization Format (OVF): an open standard for packaging and distributing virtual software</span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">vbk</span></td>
<td><a href="https://www.veeam.com/products/virtual/vmware-backup-recovery.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener"><span style="font-weight: 400;">Veeam</span></a><span style="font-weight: 400;"> Backup (VBK) file: stores backup copies of a VM's data at a specific point in time</span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">vbm</span></td>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400;">Veeam Backup Metadata (VBM) file: stores metadata about a VBK file</span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">vib</span></td>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400;">VMware Installation Bundle (VIB): a package file for installing or upgrading ESXi hosts</span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">vmdk</span></td>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400;">Virtual Machine Disk (VMDK) file: used in virtual machines like VMware and VirtualBox</span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">vmem</span></td>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400;">VMware Memory (VMEM) file: a backup of a VM's RAM content from the host system</span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">vmsd</span></td>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400;">VMware Snapshot Metadata (VMSD) file: stores metadata about each VM snapshot</span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">vmsn</span></td>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400;">VMware Snapshot State (VMSN) file: stores the running state of a VM at the time of snapshot</span></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400; font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">vswp</span></td>
<td><span style="font-weight: 400;">VMware Swap (VSWP) file: swaps memory pages to the hard drive when a host is low on physical memory</span></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><span style="font-size: 10pt;">Table 2. File extensions targeted by Mario.</span></p>
<p>Mario iterates through each of the files in the specified directory path, checking for the targeted extensions. During this iteration process, Mario ignores various entries in the directory, like <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.</span> (current directory) and <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">..</span> (parent directory).</p>
<p>The encryptor also ignores files with the following strings anywhere in the filename, even if the filename has a targeted extension:</p>
<ul>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.marion</span></li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.emario</span></li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.lmario</span></li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.nmario</span></li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.mmario</span></li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.wmario</span></li>
</ul>
<p>This exclusion is likely to avoid double-encrypting files, to avoid the possibility of the files becoming corrupted and unrecoverable.</p>
<p>Figure 4 shows the extensions from Table 2 when we tested a <a href="https://www.virustotal.com/gui/file/0fe7fcc66726f8f2daed29b807d1da3c531ec004925625855f8889950d0d24d8/details" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Mario sample</a> discovered earlier this year.</p>
<figure id="attachment_168629" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-168629" style="width: 600px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-168629 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-635577-168583-4.png" alt="Terminal screen showing a program named 'e_mario.out' running an encryption process on various files with extensions such as vmsn, vbm, vmdk, vmxf, vsv, vmsd, and vswp." width="600" height="428" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-635577-168583-4.png 1390w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-635577-168583-4-617x440.png 617w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-635577-168583-4-981x700.png 981w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-635577-168583-4-768x548.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 600px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-168629" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 4. Mario sample targeting file extensions associated with virtualization.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Targeting an organization's virtual infrastructure and backups is a known RansomHouse tactic. Both approaches are intended to inhibit data recovery if a victim does not pay the ransom.</p>
<h3><a id="post-168583-_ttnuraiywpcs"></a>Encrypting Files</h3>
<p>While encrypting targeted files, Mario displays its progress, as Figure 4 above shows. Encrypted files are renamed, appending the existing filename with an extension that includes the string <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">mario</span>. Figure 5 shows an example of <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.emario</span> as the extension for encrypted files after running a Mario sample.</p>
<figure id="attachment_168640" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-168640" style="width: 600px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-168640 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-638645-168583-5.png" alt="A screenshot of a terminal window displaying the output of the &quot;ls -a&quot; command, listing various files including ones with the suffix &quot;.emario&quot;. Highlighted in blue is the directory named &quot;test_subdirectory&quot;." width="600" height="549" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-638645-168583-5.png 1026w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-638645-168583-5-481x440.png 481w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-638645-168583-5-766x700.png 766w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-638645-168583-5-768x702.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 600px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-168640" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 5. Listing the directory content reveals encrypted files with the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.emario</span> extension.</figcaption></figure>
<h3><a id="post-168583-_taw4ld6vpfvo"></a>Reporting Statistics</h3>
<p>After Mario finishes encrypting targeted files, it displays statistics of the encryption results. These statistics, in order, are:</p>
<ul>
<li>The number of files that could not be encrypted</li>
<li>The number of files that were encrypted</li>
<li>The number of skipped files</li>
<li>The total file count</li>
<li>The amount of data that was encrypted</li>
</ul>
<p>Figure 6 shows an example of a statistics report after running a Mario sample.</p>
<figure id="attachment_168651" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-168651" style="width: 600px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-168651 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-641510-168583-6.png" alt="Screen capture of a terminal displaying the output of a file decryption process, listing statistics including encrypted files processed, skipped files, and total data tested." width="600" height="405" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-641510-168583-6.png 1390w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-641510-168583-6-652x440.png 652w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-641510-168583-6-1037x700.png 1037w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-641510-168583-6-768x518.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 600px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-168651" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 6. Example of a Mario sample reporting its encryption statistics.</figcaption></figure>
<p>While all known samples of Mario follow the same execution flow, the process is more complex in recent Mario samples. The next section reviews the differences between the earlier and later Mario samples, revealing an upgrade in Mario's encryption methods.</p>
<h2><a id="post-168583-_tykdven1nlvj"></a>Mario's Upgraded Encryption</h2>
<p>We identified two versions of Mario based on the differences in encryption routines among currently known samples. Comparing these two versions reveals that developers have updated Mario to use a substantially more complex encryption method. We refer to these two versions as:</p>
<ul>
<li>Original version</li>
<li>Upgraded version</li>
</ul>
<p>Comparing blocks of disassembled code for the encryption routine, there is a noticeably more complex block of functions in the upgraded version. Figure 7 compares the encryption code blocks for these two versions, showing noticeably more sections in the upgraded version on the right than in the original version on the left.</p>
<figure id="attachment_168662" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-168662" style="width: 900px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-168662 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-644575-168583-7.png" alt="Comparison of encryption code blocks from a sample of original Mario (left) and upgraded Mario (right), with lines and blocks highlighted in green." width="900" height="1070" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-644575-168583-7.png 1722w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-644575-168583-7-370x440.png 370w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-644575-168583-7-589x700.png 589w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-644575-168583-7-768x913.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-644575-168583-7-1292x1536.png 1292w" sizes="(max-width: 900px) 100vw, 900px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-168662" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 7. Comparison of encryption code blocks between the original and upgraded versions of Mario.</figcaption></figure>
<p>To demonstrate the upgrade in Mario's encryption, we compare code from samples of the two versions across the following functions:</p>
<ul>
<li>Encryption</li>
<li>Memory layout and buffer management</li>
<li>File processing</li>
<li>Output format</li>
</ul>
<p>Improvements in these functions make the upgraded version of Mario significantly more efficient and resilient to analysis than the original version.</p>
<h3><a id="post-168583-_u450tnyywr6g"></a>Encryption</h3>
<p>The original version of Mario has a straightforward and basic encryption routine. Figure 8 shows disassembled code from the original version. This code performs a single pass to transform a file's data from unencrypted to encrypted.</p>
<figure id="attachment_168673" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-168673" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-168673 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-648334-168583-8.png" alt="Screenshot of programming code in an IDE, featuring multiple lines of assembly language with annotations explaining each part of the code. The code includes operations like memory setting and transformation setup." width="1000" height="563" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-648334-168583-8.png 2012w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-648334-168583-8-782x440.png 782w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-648334-168583-8-1244x700.png 1244w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-648334-168583-8-768x432.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-648334-168583-8-1536x864.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-168673" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 8. Disassembled code for the original version's single-pass file transformation.</figcaption></figure>
<p>In contrast, the upgraded version of Mario features a two-stage file transformation that includes a secondary encryption key. Figure 9 shows disassembled code from a sample of the upgraded version of Mario, revealing this more complex encryption process.</p>
<figure id="attachment_168684" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-168684" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-168684 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-652326-168583-9.png" alt="Screenshot of a computer screen displaying code in an IDE with annotations explaining key encryption steps, and a flowchart diagram illustrating data processing steps on the lower right corner." width="1000" height="542" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-652326-168583-9.png 2048w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-652326-168583-9-786x426.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-652326-168583-9-1292x700.png 1292w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-652326-168583-9-768x416.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-652326-168583-9-1536x833.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-168684" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 9. Disassembled code revealing the upgraded version's more complex file transformation.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The upgraded version's code reveals a two-factor encryption scheme where the file is encrypted with both a primary key and a secondary key. Data encryption is processed separately for each key. This significantly increases the difficulty of decrypting the data without both keys.</p>
<p>Figure 10 shows that the upgraded version of Mario uses random values to generate a 32-byte primary encryption key and an 8-byte secondary encryption key.</p>
<figure id="attachment_168695" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-168695" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-168695 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-656319-168583-10.png" alt="A screenshot of a computer code snippet displaying various assembly language instructions related to cryptographic operations such as entropy generation and key management. The code includes comments for clarification on the functionality of each line." width="1000" height="446" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-656319-168583-10.png 1938w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-656319-168583-10-786x350.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-656319-168583-10-1570x700.png 1570w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-656319-168583-10-768x342.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-656319-168583-10-1536x685.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-168695" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 10. Disassembled code showing key generation used by Mario's upgraded version.</figcaption></figure>
<p>These changes represent a significant upgrade in Mario's encryption.</p>
<h3><a id="post-168583-_4zwx9ssvv5xt"></a>Memory Layout and Buffer Management</h3>
<p>When discussing memory layout and buffer management, we must understand <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/extensibility/debugger/stack-frames" target="_blank" rel="noopener">stack frames</a> and buffers. In this case, buffers are portions of the stack frame specified by an offset value.</p>
<p>The original version of Mario uses the following stack frames and buffer values during its encryption process:</p>
<ul>
<li>Upgraded version stack frame size: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">0x1408</span> bytes</li>
<li>Key buffer offsets: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">var_1400</span> (primary), <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">var_130</span> (transformation)</li>
<li>Chunk size: Fixed at <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">0xA00000</span> with no dynamic adjustments</li>
</ul>
<p>This indicates a relatively straightforward, simple process for transforming files to an encrypted state. In contrast, stack frame and buffer values for the upgraded version of Mario show a more complex structure that is smaller and more efficient:</p>
<ul>
<li>Upgraded version stack frame size: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">0x1268</span> bytes</li>
<li>Multiple buffer offsets:
<ul>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">var_1150</span>: Primary encryption context</li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">var_A0</span>: Intermediate transformation buffer</li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">var_20</span>: Secondary key storage (8 bytes)</li>
<li><span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">var_40</span>: Header storage for encrypted files</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p>These stack frame and buffer values are used in a process where:</p>
<ul>
<li>Initial data is read into the primary buffer (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">ptr</span>)</li>
<li>The data is transformed using the primary key at <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">var_1150</span></li>
<li>It is further processed with the secondary key at <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">var_20</span></li>
<li>Final encrypted data includes a header from <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">var_40</span></li>
</ul>
<p>The careful organization of these buffers confirms the layered approach of Mario's upgraded version.</p>
<h3><a id="post-168583-_y35xpu65svqi"></a>File Processing</h3>
<p>Mario's original version uses a straightforward approach to file processing. It's a linear process that encrypts the files as sequential fixed-size segments in a loop. After encrypting each segment, the code checks if the combined size of the processed segments exceeds a specified threshold. Once it passes that threshold, the code jumps from the loop to a different function.</p>
<p>Figure 11 illustrates this linear process in the disassembled code.</p>
<figure id="attachment_168706" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-168706" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-168706 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-659834-168583-11.png" alt="Screenshot of a computer code in an IDE, displaying lines for file size comparison and conditional jumps with comments." width="1000" height="268" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-659834-168583-11.png 2048w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-659834-168583-11-786x211.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-659834-168583-11-1920x515.png 1920w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-659834-168583-11-768x206.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-659834-168583-11-1536x412.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-168706" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 11. Disassembled code showing a linear process for encryption in Mario's original version.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Code in Mario's upgraded version reveals an encryption method that uses chunk processing with dynamic sizing. Figure 12 shows an example.</p>
<figure id="attachment_168717" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-168717" style="width: 900px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-168717 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-663272-168583-12.png" alt="A screenshot of assembly language code displayed in a text editor with highlighted syntax. The code includes various operations such as move, shift, and multiply with registers and constants." width="900" height="1286" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-663272-168583-12.png 1433w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-663272-168583-12-308x440.png 308w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-663272-168583-12-490x700.png 490w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-663272-168583-12-768x1098.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-663272-168583-12-1075x1536.png 1075w" sizes="(max-width: 900px) 100vw, 900px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-168717" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 12. Disassembled code showing chunked processing with dynamic for encryption in Mario's upgraded version.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Comparing the processing logic between these two versions, we find significant differences.</p>
<p>Mario's original version uses a simpler programming loop that processes files in fixed segment lengths up to a threshold of 536,870,911 bytes, as noted in Figure 11. This version simply reports when the encryption is complete without showing any progress.</p>
<p>In comparison, Mario's upgraded version implements a more robust file processing scheme for encryption that uses:</p>
<ul>
<li>Variable segment lengths, with a size threshold of 8 GB</li>
<li>Calculations to determine chunk size and offsets</li>
<li>A sparse encryption technique where it encrypts only certain blocks of a file at specific offsets</li>
</ul>
<p>In addition, the upgraded version of Mario displays the progress of encrypting chunks of each file, as noted below in Figure 13.</p>
<figure id="attachment_168728" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-168728" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-168728 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-668221-168583-13.png" alt="A screenshot of computer code on a dark background with syntax highlighting, indicating variables and a string that includes 'Processed chunk.&quot; " width="1000" height="93" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-668221-168583-13.png 2048w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-668221-168583-13-786x73.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-668221-168583-13-1920x179.png 1920w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-668221-168583-13-768x72.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-668221-168583-13-1536x143.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-168728" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 13. Disassembled code in the upgraded version of Mario to display the progress of chunk processing.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The chunked processing of Mario's upgraded version makes static analysis more difficult because:</p>
<ul>
<li>It processes files non-linearly</li>
<li>It uses complex mathematical formulas to determine processing order</li>
<li>It employs different strategies based on file size</li>
</ul>
<h3><a id="post-168583-_e848oy40yxnv"></a>Output Format</h3>
<p>In addition to displaying the processed chunks of files when encrypting them, Mario's upgraded version also provides a more detailed summary when the encryption of each file is finished.</p>
<p>As previously stated, the original version simply reports that the encryption of a file is finished. Figure 14 shows this in the disassembled code.</p>
<figure id="attachment_168739" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-168739" style="width: 800px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-168739 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-671001-168583-14.png" alt="A screenshot of computer code with syntax highlighting, displaying various commands and a variable named 'aDoneS'. The text has a dark background and includes colors such as purple and orange for highlighting." width="800" height="116" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-671001-168583-14.png 1128w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-671001-168583-14-786x114.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-671001-168583-14-768x112.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 800px) 100vw, 800px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-168739" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 14. Code from the original version of Mario to report when a file is finished processing.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Mario's upgraded version includes more information when each file is finished processing, as Figure 15 below shows in the disassembled code.</p>
<figure id="attachment_168750" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-168750" style="width: 700px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-168750 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-673614-168583-15.png" alt="Screenshot of computer code in an IDE, highlighting the command 'aDoneSLdLdLdLd' in a purple box." width="700" height="56" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-673614-168583-15.png 1708w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-673614-168583-15-786x63.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-673614-168583-15-768x61.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-673614-168583-15-1536x122.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 700px) 100vw, 700px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-168750" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 15. Code from the upgraded version of Mario to report when a file is finished processing.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Ultimately, the core functionality of these two Mario samples (the original version and the upgraded version) remains the same. Both samples encrypt files and rename them by adding <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.emario</span> extension. But the upgraded version implements a more complex and potentially more secure encryption methodology with selective file processing.</p>
<h2><a id="post-168583-_xzylt0gjnup2"></a>Conclusion</h2>
<p>The upgrade in encryption used by RansomHouse RaaS, going from a simple linear model to a more complex multi-layered approach, signals a concerning trajectory in ransomware development. This demonstrates how threat actors are updating their techniques to enhance effectiveness.</p>
<p>This upgrade is built on several key technical improvements:</p>
<ul>
<li>A two-factor encryption scheme that significantly increases the difficulty of decryption without both keys</li>
<li>Chunked file processing with dynamic sizing instead of a simpler method</li>
<li>The new file processing makes static analysis and reverse engineering more challenging</li>
</ul>
<p>Threat actors could view this as a useful path for future ransomware variants. As other ransomware groups adopt these more sophisticated methods, the ransomware threat landscape will become more resilient to security controls. This upgrade underscores the need to adopt more dynamic, adaptive strategies capable of countering the next generation of complex and evasive threats.</p>
<p>Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed above through the following products:</p>
<ul>
<li>The <a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/wildfire" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced WildFire</a> machine-learning models and analysis techniques have been reviewed and updated in light of the indicators shared in this research.</li>
<li><a href="https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/cortex/cortex-xpanse" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cortex Xpanse</a> and the <a href="https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/cortex/cortex-xsiam" target="_blank" rel="noopener">ASM add-on for XSIAM</a> provide detection of VMware ESXi infrastructure exposed to the public internet via “VMware ESXi” and “Insecure VMware ESXi” attack surface rules. In addition to these, there is also a post-compromise detection attack surface rule for “ESXiArgs Ransomware Infection.” This can detect ransom notes injected by malicious actors, as well as other indicators of ransomware infection impacting internet-exposed ESXi servers.</li>
</ul>

                  <a class="card-category" href="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/category/threat-actor-groups/" role="link" data-page-track="true" data-page-track-value="ransomhouse-encryption-upgrade:related-resources:Threat Actor Groups Tracked by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 (Updated Aug. 1, 2025):Threat Actor Groups"><span class=""><img src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/threat-actor-groups.svg" alt=" category icon">Threat Actor Groups</span></a>                        <span class="post-pub-date"><time datetime="2025-08-01T13:00:15+00:00">August 1, 2025</time></span>
                  <a href="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/threat-actor-groups-tracked-by-palo-alto-networks-unit-42/" data-page-track="true" data-page-track-value="ransomhouse-encryption-upgrade:related-resources:Threat Actor Groups Tracked by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 (Updated Aug. 1, 2025)">
                    <h4 class="post-title">Threat Actor Groups Tracked by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 (Updated Aug. 1, 2025)</h4>
                  </a>

<script>

(function($) {
	// Migrated from the unit42-v5 + Modifications
	var subscribeSuccess = false;
	var email = document.getElementById('newsletter-email');
	var subscription_form = document.getElementById('unit42footerSubscription_form');
	var subscription_form_button = document.getElementById('unit42footerSubscription_form_button');
	window.captchaComplete = function() {
		subscribeSuccess = true;
		if ($(mail).val() != '' && isEmail($(mail).val())) {
			$(subscription_form_button).removeClass('is-disabled');
		}
		setTimeout(function() {
			$(email).focus();
			$('.g-recaptcha iframe').attr('tabindex', '-1');
		}, 100)
	}
	window.captchaExpires = function() {
		subscribeSuccess = false;
		$(subscription_form_button).addClass('is-disabled', true);
	} 
	$(subscription_form).submit(function(e) {
		e.preventDefault();
		e.stopImmediatePropagation();
		updateEmailMask();
		var success = true;
		var form = $(this);
		var mail = form.find('input[name="Email"]');
		
		if (mail.val() === '') {
			mail.addClass('has-error');
			showError(1);
			success = false;	
		}  else if (!isEmail(mail.val())){
			showError(2);
			success = false;
		}
		else {
			mail.removeClass('has-error');
			$('.error-mail').addClass('d-none');
		}

		if (!subscribeSuccess) {
			$('.error-recaptcha').removeClass('d-none');
		} else {
			$('.error-recaptcha').addClass('d-none');
		}

		if (success && subscribeSuccess) {
			$.ajax({
				type: 'POST',
				url: form.attr('action'),
				data: form.serialize(),
				beforeSend: function() {
                 form.find('button').addClass('is-loading');
    			},
				success: function(msg) {
					form.find('.form-success-message').html('<p class="success-message">You have been successfully subscribed</p>');
					form.find('button').removeClass('is-loading');
					$(email).val('');
					clearError();
				},
				error: function(jqXHR, textStatus, errorThrown) {
					$(subscription_form_button).addClass('is-disabled', true);
					form.find('button').removeClass('is-loading');
					
				}
			});
		}
		return false;
	});
	function showError(error_type){
		if(error_type == 1) {
			$('.error-mail').text("Please enter the email address.").addClass('error-show');
			$(subscription_form_button).addClass('is-disabled');
		} else if(error_type == 2){
			$('.error-mail').text("Please provide a valid e-mail address.").addClass('error-show');
			$(subscription_form_button).addClass('is-disabled');
		}	
		$(subscription_form_button).removeClass('is-loading');
	}
	function clearError(){
		$('.error-mail').text("").removeClass('error-show');;
		$(subscription_form_button).removeClass('is-loading');
		$(subscription_form_button).removeClass('is-disabled');
	}
	
	$(email).on('input', function (event) { 
		var email = $(this).val();
		if (isEmail(email) ) {			
			clearError();
		} else if(email == ""){
			clearError();
		} else{
			showError(2);			  
		}
    });

	function isEmail(email) {
		var re = /^(([^<>()\[\]\\.,;:\s@"]+(\.[^<>()\[\]\\.,;:\s@"]+)*)|(".+"))@((\[[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\])|(([a-zA-Z\-0-9]+\.)+[a-zA-Z]{2,}))$/;
		return re.test(String(email).toLowerCase());
	}
	
	var captcha_loaded = false;
         if(!captcha_loaded){
            // recaptcha on foucs call
            $(document).on('change paste keyup', '#newsletter-email', function () {
               if($('.g-recaptcha').hasClass('d-none')){
                $('.g-recaptcha').removeClass('d-none');
               }
               if(!captcha_loaded ){
                  captcha_loaded  = true;
                  // trigger loading api.js (recaptcha.js) script
                  var head = document.getElementsByTagName('head')[0];
                  var script = document.createElement('script');
                  script.type = 'text/javascript';
                  script.src = 'https://www.google.com/recaptcha/api.js?hl=en_US';
                  head.appendChild(script);
               }
            });
        }
	
	function updateEmailMask() {
		var email = $("#unit42footerSubscription_form input[name='Email']").val();
		if (email && email.trim() != '') {
			var maskedEmail = maskEmailAddress(email);
			$("#unit42footerSubscription_form input[name='emailFormMask']").val(maskedEmail);
		}
	}

	function maskEmailAddress (emailAddress) {
		function mask(str) {
			var strLen = str.length;
			if (strLen > 4) {
				return str.substr(0, 1) + str.substr(1, strLen - 1).replace(/\w/g, '*') + str.substr(-1,1);
			}
			return str.replace(/\w/g, '*');
		}
		return emailAddress.replace(/([\w.]+)@([\w.]+)(\.[\w.]+)/g, function (m, p1, p2, p3) {
			return mask(p1) + '@' + mask(p2) + p3;
		});

		return emailAddress;
	}

}(jQuery));
//# sourceMappingURL=main.js.map
	
</script>

<script type="text/javascript">
	$(document).ready(function(){
		$("html").on("click", ".language-btn", function () {
			$(this).toggleClass("expand");
			$(".language-dropdown").toggleClass("expand");
		});

		$("html").on("click", "body", function (b) {
			if (!$(b.target).is(".language-btn")) {
				$(".language-btn").removeClass("expand");
				$(".language-dropdown").removeClass("expand");
			}
		});
	});

	var isProcessing = false; 
    function alter_ul_post_values(obj,post_id,ul_type){
	
		if (isProcessing)    
		return;  
		isProcessing = true;   
		var like_nonce = jQuery('#_wpnonce').val();
		jQuery(obj).find("span").html("..");
                jQuery.ajax({
                    type: "POST",
                    url: "https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/plugins/like-dislike-counter-for-posts-pages-and-comments/ajax_counter.php",
                    data: "post_id="+post_id+"&up_type="+ul_type+"&ul_nonce="+like_nonce,
                    success: function(msg){
                            jQuery(obj).find("span").html(msg);
                            isProcessing = false; 
                            jQuery(obj).find('svg').children('path').attr('stroke','#0050FF');
                            jQuery(obj).removeClass('idc_ul_cont_not_liked idc_ul_cont_not_liked_inner');
                    }
 		});
	}

function loadScript(url, defer){
    var script1 = document.createElement('script');
    script1.setAttribute('type', 'text/javascript');
    script1.setAttribute('src',url);
    if(defer == true){
        script1.setAttribute('defer','defer');
    }
    document.head.appendChild(script1);
}
function loadScript1(url, callback){

    var script = document.createElement("script")
    script.type = "text/javascript";
    if (script.readyState){  //IE
        script.onreadystatechange = function(){
            if (script.readyState == "loaded" || script.readyState == "complete"){
                script.onreadystatechange = null;
                callback();
            }
        };
    } else {  //Others
        script.onload = function(){
            callback();
        };
    }
    script.src = url;
    document.getElementsByTagName("head")[0].appendChild(script);
}
if(referer == "CloudCortex" || referer == "Prisma" || referer == "Cortex" || referer == "Sase" || referer == "Unit" || referer == "Ngfw"){
	if(referer == "Unit"){
    setTimeout(function(){
      loadScript(main_site_criticalTopBase, false);
      loadScript1(main_site_criticalTopProductNav, function(){
        window.PAN_initializeProduct2021Nav();
      });
      loadScript(main_site_defered, false);
    }, 3000);
	}
	else{
    setTimeout(function(){
      loadScript1(main_site_critical_top, function(){
        window.PAN_initializeProduct2021Nav();
      });
      loadScript(main_site_defered, false);
    }, 3000);
	}
}

document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function() {
  // Find all the forms on the page
  var forms = document.getElementsByTagName("form");

  // Loop through each form
  for (var i = 0; i < forms.length; i++) {
    var form = forms[i];

    // Check if the hidden input field already exists
    var requestInput = form.querySelector("input[name='web_unit42_req_id']");
    if (!requestInput) {
      // Create a hidden input element if it doesn't exist
      requestInput = document.createElement("input");
      requestInput.type = "hidden";
      requestInput.name = "web_unit42_req_id";
      requestInput.id = "web_unit42_req_id";

      // Append the hidden field to the form
      form.appendChild(requestInput);
    }
  }
});

// Assign the onCheqResponse function to the window object to handle events from any form
window.onCheqResponse = function(encryptedMessage, requestID) {
  // Find all the forms on the page
  var forms = document.getElementsByTagName("form");

  for (var i = 0; i < forms.length; i++) {
    var form = forms[i];
    var requestInput = form.querySelector("input[name='web_unit42_req_id']");
    if (requestInput) {
      requestInput.value = requestID;
    }
  }
};

</script>
